candidates.attacker_control: The expression text is stored in a dashboard widget configuration (`dataSourceProperties`, e.g. `queryConditions[].queryValue`) written via the management API (`POST/PUT /api/management/v1/dashboard/{dashboardKey}/widget-configuration[/{widgetKey}]`) or supplied through deployed dashboard configuration JSON. It is later deserialized (`objectMapper.treeToValue(config.dataSourceProperties, …)`, DashboardDataService.kt:88) and handed to the data-source method, so the payload survives until data retrieval. The trivial validation gate does not prevent an arbitrary SpEL payload that also contains `localDateTimeNow` (e.g. as a trailing command argument or a comment inside the command string).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and discounted: the `${null}` and `${currentUserId}`/permission-condition values are handled before the SpEL branch, so only values containing `localDateTimeNow` reach the parser; the root object only exposes `localDateTimeNow`, which limits property traversal but does not restrict `T(...)` type access or method invocation; the post-evaluation conversion to LocalDateTime throws, but execution already happened; no `SimpleEvaluationContext`/`FunctionReference`/allowlist use exists anywhere in the repository (searched). Looked for a lower-privileged write path to widget configuration: `DashboardService.createWidgetConfiguration/updateWidgetConfiguration(s)` are only called from `AdminDashboardResource` and all dashboard management routes require ROLE_ADMIN in `DashboardHttpSecurityConfigurer`; the case-level widget-tab flow (`CaseWidgetTabService`) uses JsonPath/ValueResolver-based providers, not this SpEL sink. I could not verify a non-admin or unauthenticated path to set `queryValue` in the snapshot.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution with the application's privileges (JVM/OS command execution via java.lang.Runtime/ProcessBuilder type references), plus disclosure/tampering of data the application can reach. Because the expression is persisted in widget configuration, it is stored rather than reflected, and it is re-executed each time the affected widget data is requested. With the default deployment the entry point is an administrative configuration API, so the immediate privilege boundary is admin-to-OS within the Valtimo application; where the management API or dashboard configuration is exposed to less-trusted operators/configurations, the boundary is lower.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) The dashboard module is enabled (default in this distribution) with a widget using data sources `case-count`/`case-counts`/`case-group-by` (`DocumentWidgetDataSource`); (2) the attacker can create/update the widget configuration — in the shipped security configuration this requires ROLE_ADMIN authority (`DashboardHttpSecurityConfigurer` lines 36-48) or control over a deployed dashboard configuration file; (3) a user (any user with permission to view the dashboard) triggers data retrieval, causing the stored expression to be evaluated. No network position beyond normal API access; the payload must not contain a `}` before the end of the expression because of the `substringBefore("}")` truncation.
candidates.root_cause: QueryCondition.queryValue is used to build a SpEL expression with only a weak substring gate (`queryValueIsDateTimeSpelExpression`, QueryCondition.kt:82-86: value must start with `${`, end with `}`, and contain the literal text `localDateTimeNow`). The substring check can be satisfied by attacker-chosen text, after which the text between the first `${` and the first `}` is parsed by `SpelExpressionParser` and evaluated through `StandardEvaluationContext` (QueryCondition.kt:94-107). The evaluation context restricts neither type references (`T(...)`) nor method invocation and uses only the default type locator, so `java.lang` classes (e.g. Runtime/ProcessBuilder) remain reachable. There is no allowlist that the expression is exactly the intended `localDateTimeNow` variable.
candidates.title: SpEL injection in dashboard/widget query condition (QueryCondition) evaluated from configured queryValue
candidates.trace: GET /api/v1/dashboard/{dashboardKey}/data (DashboardResource.getDashboardData, authenticated) -> DashboardDataService.getWidgetDataForDashboard (line 49) -> getWidgetDataByConfig (line 76) -> resolves the `@WidgetDataSource` method via WidgetDataSourceResolver and reflects it (`method.invoke`, line 92) -> DocumentWidgetDataSource.getCaseCount/getCaseCounts/getCaseGroupBy (document module, lines 38-102) -> QueryCondition.toPredicate -> queryValueIsDateTimeSpelExpression matches -> SpelExpressionParser.parseExpression(value between `${` and first `}`) -> StandardEvaluationContext.getValue(context, LocalDateTime.class) executes the expression's side effects before the expected type conversion fails.
candidates.unverified: Not executed or dynamically confirmed: exploitability depends on (a) which roles/API access a given deployment grants to the dashboard management endpoints or deployment configuration, and (b) whether the payload's command construction avoids `}` before the end of the expression (a practical constraint, bypassable with single-command plus-argument forms such as `exec('cmd arg1 arg2 localDateTimeNow')`). I did not verify the runtime SpEL type-locator behaviour in this exact Spring version, nor that a concrete data source bean is present in every deployment.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-917 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an Expression Language Statement ('Expression Language Injection') / CWE-94 Code Injection

coverage_summary: Source scope: 3,089 readable files under the assigned root (source_root_files=3,089; 0 excluded for size/sensitivity; binary-like files are refused/skipped). The snapshot contains only production sources (`src/main`) plus build/config/changelog resources — no test sources — so test-implied behaviour could not be used as evidence. P1 relation scope: 3,081 files indexed, 8 files missing from the index, 685 Java files parsed, 0 parse errors, 5,663 symbols/9,166 call sites; capabilities explicitly exclude control flow, data flow, semantic resolution and runtime reachability, and 6,719 calls are unresolved, so index edges were used only for navigation and every cited candidate was verified in source text. Modules/files inspected in source (non-exhaustive): core JWT/security configurers and HTTP filter chain, Casemunda task/process services, document search/specification/dialect helpers, PBAC authorization module (service, specifications, denials, permission conditions), MyBatis mapper XML and order-by helpers, case/case-tab/case-widget modules, dashboard module (resources, services, widget data sources, QueryCondition), notes, form/form-flow/form-view-model, resource (temporary storage, openzaak/local resources), importer/exporter, zgw (objecten/documenten/zaken/catalogi/besluiten/notificaties/portaaltaak/object-management), objects-api, data-provider, value-resolver, plugin service, audit, logging, search, localization and the sample app configuration/permission files. Areas sampled but not exhaustively audited: every module's security configurer list (about 100 classes), Liquibase changelogs, mail/connector/klant/haalcentraal/exact-plugin/portaaltaak-specific processing, and all frontend-adjacent JSON configuration.
limitations: No code was executed, no application was started, no scanner/SAST/ground-truth data was consulted, and no index label was treated as a vulnerability verdict; the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

The P1 index is syntax-only (no control flow, no data flow, no semantic resolution, 6,719 unresolved calls) and 8 files are missing from it; therefore reachability, bean wiring and authentication state could not be proven by the index and were reasoned from source text only.

Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so negative/positive unit tests that might confirm or refute intended behaviour (e.g. that `localDateTimeNow` is meant to be the only supported expression) could not be inspected.

Spring Security request-matcher semantics and Spring Expression Language type-locator behaviour were reasoned from source and framework knowledge, not exercised; a deployment that does not expose the dashboard management API to lower-privileged users, or that blocks `T(...)` through a custom configuration, would reduce the candidate's reachability.

The 1-candidate output cap means other plausible but weaker leads (SSRF via plugin-URL prefix matching, coarse ResourcePermission checks on Documenten API endpoints, configuration-dependent cross-case note/widget reads, XXE/privacy questions in BPMN parsing) were recorded as rejected leads rather than fully investigated.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF / credential leak via prefix-based plugin lookup: `ObjectenApiPlugin.findConfigurationByUrl` (and equivalent `startsWith` checks in zaken/documenten/besluiten/catalogi/objecttypen plugins) combined with user-supplied absolute URLs on `GET /api/v1/object?objectUrl=` (ObjectResource.getObjectByUrl, ZaakObjectService.getObjectByObjectUrl, ObjectenApiClient.getObject which requests the full URI with the plugin's authentication applied).
rejected_leads.reason: Real validation weakness (string prefix match instead of scheme/host comparison), but the bypass (host-suffix or userinfo URL such as `https://configured-host@evil.tld/…`) only works when the configured plugin URL has no trailing path/slash, which the snapshot does not establish; the pattern is systemic across six plugins and therefore looks like upstream design rather than a single fixable defect. Impact also depends on module/plugin configuration.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing object-level authorization on Documenten API file endpoints: `GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/documenten-api/{pluginConfigurationId}/files/{documentId}[/download]` require only `authenticated()` in `DocumentenApiHttpSecurityConfigurer`; `DocumentenApiService`/`DocumentenApiClient` enforce only a coarse `ResourcePermission` VIEW/MODIFY/DELETE with no case/document context.
rejected_leads.reason: The shipped default permission file grants `view`/`delete` on ResourcePermission only to ROLE_ADMIN (ROLE_USER gets view_list/create), so with default configuration the coarse check blocks ROLE_USER; the residual risk is a configuration/design concern (application-defined permissions) rather than a demonstrable bypass in the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Cross-case data exposure under shipped default permissions: `NoteService.getNotes(documentId)` (note view_list granted unconditionally to ROLE_USER in `app/gzac/.../note.permission.json`) and `CaseWidgetTabService.getWidgetTab/getCaseWidgetData` (CaseWidgetTabWidget VIEW with empty conditions) read notes/widget data for arbitrary document IDs without a document-level check.
rejected_leads.reason: Authorization is delegated to the PBAC permission documents; the sample configuration grants these permissions without conditions, and the library exposes context hooks (NoteDocumentMapper, AuthorizationResourceContext) intended to be configured. This is a configuration-dependent weakness rather than clearly defective library logic, so it was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in `ProcessShortTimerService.createDocumentFrom` (DocumentBuilderFactory.newDefaultInstance without disallowing DOCTYPE/external entities) when the stored BPMN process model is parsed by `PUT /api/v1/process/definition/{processDefinitionId}/xml/timer`.
rejected_leads.reason: The XML input is the server-side stored process model that was previously deployed (deployment endpoint requires ROLE_ADMIN), so exploitation requires an administrator to have deployed attacker-controlled BPMN; lower immediate impact and stronger prerequisites than the selected candidate. Not verified whether Camunda/JDK defaults block external entity resolution here.

rejected_leads.lead: Potential missing authorization on deprecated resource download: `OpenZaakResource.getContent` (`GET /api/v1/resource/{resourceId}/download`, authenticated only) fetches document content from the Documenten API by resource UUID without any permission check (unlike the newer DocumentenApiClient which requires ResourcePermission.VIEW).
rejected_leads.reason: Deprecated since 12.0.0 and only relevant when the openzaak-resource module is active; resource UUIDs are random and normally only visible inside authorized case data, so the object-level exposure requires prior knowledge of an identifier. Source-verifiable but weaker impact/attacker path than the selected candidate.

summary: Repository snapshot: Valtimo backend libraries v12.8.0 (Ritense), ~3,089 files (Java/Kotlin, Gradle, JSON/YAML config, Liquibase XML, MyBatis XML). This is a large multi-module Spring Boot/Camunda application; I traced authorization plumbing (PBAC authorization module, ~100 HttpSecurityConfigurer classes), the Stored-Query/JSON search paths, ZGW integration modules, importer/exporter, resource storage, form/form-flow, dashboard widgets and security/crypto classes. The strongest single source-evidenced issue I found is an unsafe SpEL evaluation of a dashboard/widget query value: `QueryCondition.toPredicate` treats the configured `queryValue` as a SpEL expression whenever it merely contains the substring "localDateTimeNow", parses it with `SpelExpressionParser` and evaluates it with a `StandardEvaluationContext` (no `SimpleEvaluationContext`, no type/method restrictions, and no allowlist of the intended `localDateTimeNow` variable). A crafted value such as `${T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('… localDateTimeNow')}` passes the substring/startsWith/endsWith check, executes during evaluation, and only afterwards fails conversion to LocalDateTime — a classic expression-language injection (CWE-917/94). Because the value is persisted with a widget configuration and executed later whenever the dashboard/widget data is requested, this is a stored-code-execution sink. Rejected/weaker leads are listed below (SSRF via plugin-URL prefix matching, coarse ResourcePermission-only checks on Documenten API file endpoints, cross-case reads of notes/widget-tab data under the shipped default permission files, unguarded JAXP parser in ProcessShortTimerService).
